meta.prompt_suffix: Style: candid documentary photograph of a real place, not an advertisement, not CGI, not a composite. Screens, tickers and backlit signs are allowed to be bright because they physically emit light, but nothing is post-processed to glow — no bloom, no rim light, no lens flare, no HDR look, no hyper-saturation, no studio lighting on the person. thumbnails.prompt_en: COMPOSITION RULE, HIGHEST PRIORITY: the photograph fills the entire 16:9 frame edge to edge with a real scene — never a letterbox band, never an empty panel, never a flat colour block, and never a large expanse of bare empty floor. The bottom three-eighths of the frame height is filled by the dark backs and shoulders of the seated customers nearest the camera, so far out of focus and so deeply in shadow that it reads as one single dark mass with no readable detail, which keeps overlay text legible on top of it. No face, no hand, no screen and no bright object sits in that bottom three-eighths — every face, hand, sign and key object sits in the upper five-eighths. Counters and table tops run across the MIDDLE of the frame, never near the bottom edge, and anything resting on them sits at mid height. SCALE, EQUALLY IMPORTANT: the man in his early sixties is the largest thing in the picture — his head and shoulders occupy the entire right third of the frame, his face alone spans roughly the top 55 to 60 percent of the frame height, the top of his hair touches the upper edge and is very slightly cropped by it, and his shoulder leaves the frame on the right. The other people are far smaller, roughly one third of his head height. TEXT SIZE, CRITICAL: every Korean word and number quoted below is rendered LARGE — each character at least one twelfth of the frame height, thick and high-contrast, filling most of the width of the sign, banner or screen it sits on, so it is still readable when the whole picture is shrunk to 160 by 90 pixels. Banners, boards and phone screens are drawn oversized for that reason: a banner spans at least half the frame width, and a phone screen is at least one quarter of the frame height. Small print, secondary rows and background lettering are left illegible. Photographed from the back of the waiting hall of a Korean securities branch late on a weekday afternoon, camera at standing eye level. A wide wall-mounted trading board runs across the middle of the frame: its header reads "반도체" in Korean Hangul in large white characters, a red line drops steeply across the panel beside it, and the figure "-46%" sits in red at the end of that line. Rows of customers in their fifties and sixties sit under the board, tiny beside the man, two of them with both hands clasped behind their heads and one leaning forward onto his knees. The man stands at the right edge in a worn grey zip-up jacket, black hair greying at the temples, holding his phone up raised up beside the face inside the upper five-eighths and turned slightly toward the camera: the screen reads "총평가손익" in Korean Hangul on the upper line and "-92,000,000" in large red digits under it, the phone's own backlight the brightest thing on his side of the picture. Ordinary room details make it real — a stainless cup left on an armrest, a taped paper strip on the pillar, tangled cabling under the board, scuffed vinyl flooring. His lower lip is rolled inward and bitten, two vertical creases stand between his eyebrows, his eyelids are lowered but his eyes stay locked on his own phone rather than the big board, and the tendons stand out on the back of the hand gripping the phone with the knuckles gone pale.
